mentions.quote: A Brahmana who serves his guru until the dissolution of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahma.
mentions.role: cosmic destination for the devoted student

entities.description: The supreme creator deity whose eternal abode is the ultimate reward for a Brahmana who faithfully serves his guru for life.
entities.justification: Brahma is named as a deity and destination in Mn_2.244, making him a named divine figure in the text.

mentions.quote: By marrying a Shudra woman, a Brahmana falls, according to Atri and the son of Utathya
mentions.role: cited authority on the consequences of inter-varna marriage

entities.description: Vedic sage cited as an authority on the degradation of a Brahmana who marries a Shudra woman.
entities.justification: Atri is named in Mn_3.16 as one of several ancient sages whose legal opinions are invoked.

mentions.quote: according to Atri and the son of Utathya
mentions.role: cited authority on the consequences of inter-varna marriage

entities.description: Vedic sage (referred to as 'son of Utathya', likely Dīrghatamas) cited alongside Atri as an authority on the fall of a Brahmana who marries a Shudra woman.
entities.justification: The son of Utathya is named in Mn_3.16 as a distinct legal authority whose ruling is quoted.

mentions.quote: by begetting a son on her, according to Shaunaka
mentions.role: cited authority on the degree of degradation from fathering a son on a Shudra woman

entities.description: Vedic sage cited in Mn_3.16 whose ruling specifies that the degradation of a Brahmana occurs at the stage of begetting a son on a Shudra wife.
entities.justification: Shaunaka is named as an explicit textual authority in Mn_3.16 on the graded fall from Brahmanhood.

mentions.quote: and by having a son from her, according to Bhrigu
mentions.role: cited authority distinguishing the final stage of degradation

entities.description: Vedic sage cited in Mn_3.16 as an authority who holds that having a living son from a Shudra wife is the threshold of full degradation from Brahmanhood.
entities.justification: Bhrigu is named in Mn_3.16 as one of four named sages whose graduated legal opinions are contrasted.

mentions.quote: Whatever merit has been declared by Manu for each of these marriages, hear it all, O sages
mentions.role: declared authority whose rulings on marriage merit are being conveyed

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver whose pronouncements on the merit of the eight forms of marriage are the very content being transmitted in chapter 3.
entities.justification: Manu is invoked in Mn_3.36 as the authoritative source of the marriage-merit rulings being recited to the sages.

mentions.quote: A pupil who desires the highest state should not dwell permanently with a non-Brahmana guru, nor with a Brahmana who has not studied the Veda.
mentions.role: the priestly class whose qualified members alone are suitable as permanent gurus

mentions.quote: A Brahmana who serves his guru until the dissolution of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahma.
mentions.role: subject of the rule about lifelong guru-service

mentions.quote: A knower of Dharma should not give any gift to his guru beforehand
mentions.role: implied actor observing ritual graduation protocol

mentions.quote: By marrying a Shudra woman, a Brahmana falls, according to Atri and the son of Utathya
mentions.role: subject of inter-varna marriage prohibition and degradation ruling

mentions.quote: Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of a low caste, quickly degrade their families and their descendants to the state of Shudras.
mentions.role: those who transgress varna endogamy

mentions.quote: In no sacred text whatsoever is a Shudra woman ordained as a wife for a Brahmana or a Kshatriya
mentions.role: upper-varna men prohibited from Shudra wives

entities.description: The priestly varna, highest of the four social orders, whose members are the primary addressees of the rules governing studentship, marriage, and ritual purity in these chapters.
entities.justification: Brahmanas are the most frequently addressed social group across both chapters, with rules specifically governing their conduct as students, gurus, and householders.

mentions.quote: In no sacred text whatsoever is a Shudra woman ordained as a wife for a Brahmana or a Kshatriya
mentions.role: the lowest varna whose women are prohibited as wives for upper-varna men

mentions.quote: quickly degrade their families and their descendants to the state of Shudras
mentions.role: marker of social-ritual degradation

mentions.quote: A Brahmana who takes a Shudra woman to his bed sinks to a lower state
mentions.role: subject of the pollution rule

mentions.quote: A Shudra woman is for a Shudra
mentions.role: endogamous norm prescribed for the Shudra varna

entities.description: The lowest of the four varnas, whose women are explicitly prohibited as wives for Brahmanas and Kshatriyas; marriage to a Shudra woman by an upper-varna man entails graduated ritual degradation.
entities.justification: Shudras are repeatedly named as the limit-case varna in the marriage-prohibition rules of chapter 3 (Mn_3.13-19).

mentions.quote: In no sacred text whatsoever is a Shudra woman ordained as a wife for a Brahmana or a Kshatriya
mentions.role: second varna prohibited from Shudra wives

mentions.quote: she and one of his own varna for a Vaishya; these two and one of his own varna for a Kshatriya
mentions.role: subject of the graduated hypogamy rule

mentions.quote: the last four for a Kshatriya
mentions.role: varna for whom specific marriage forms are prescribed

mentions.quote: the Rākṣasa alone for a Kshatriya
mentions.role: varna for whom the Rakshasa marriage is specifically endorsed

mentions.quote: An arrow should be taken by a Kshatriya bride
mentions.role: varna-specific wedding ritual object

entities.description: The warrior-noble varna, second in rank, for whom the Rakshasa marriage form is declared lawful and who may marry women of the Vaishya and Shudra varnas.
entities.justification: Kshatriyas are addressed as a distinct varna across multiple verses in chapter 3 governing both marriage forms and wedding rituals.

mentions.quote: she and one of his own varna for a Vaishya
mentions.role: middle varna for whom Shudra and own-varna wives are permitted

mentions.quote: those same ones, excluding the Rākṣasa, are lawful for a Vaishya and a Shudra
mentions.role: varna for whom certain marriage forms are prescribed and one excluded

mentions.quote: the Āsura for a Vaishya and a Shudra
mentions.role: varna for whom the Asura marriage is declared appropriate

mentions.quote: a goad by a Vaishya bride
mentions.role: varna-specific wedding ritual object

entities.description: The merchant-cultivator varna for whom the Asura marriage is declared appropriate and who may marry women of the Shudra varna.
entities.justification: Vaishyas appear alongside Kshatriyas and Shudras in the chapter 3 regulations governing permitted marriage forms and wedding rites.

mentions.quote: the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa; and the eighth and lowest, the Paiśāca
mentions.role: listed as one of the eight marriage forms

mentions.quote: The Gāndharva and Rākṣasa marriages, whether performed separately or mixed, are declared to be lawful for a Kshatriya.
mentions.role: declared lawful form for Kshatriyas

mentions.quote: The voluntary union of a maiden and her lover is to be known as the Gāndharva rite, which springs from desire and has sexual union as its purpose.
mentions.role: defined as voluntary union based on mutual desire

entities.description: One of the eight forms of marriage—the voluntary union of a couple based on mutual desire—named after the celestial Gandharvas and declared lawful for Kshatriyas.
entities.justification: The Gandharva marriage is defined and evaluated across Mn_3.21, 3.26, and 3.32 as a recognized legal category of matrimonial union.

mentions.quote: the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa; and the eighth and lowest, the Paiśāca
mentions.role: listed as one of the eight marriage forms

mentions.quote: the Rākṣasa alone for a Kshatriya
mentions.role: declared the sole praiseworthy form for Kshatriyas

mentions.quote: The forcible abduction of a maiden from her home, while she cries out and weeps, after her kinsmen have been slain, wounded, and their houses broken into, is called the Rākṣasa form of marriage.
mentions.role: defined as violent abduction

entities.description: The marriage by forcible abduction named after the Rakshasas (demons), defined as seizing a bride by violence, and declared the sole praiseworthy marriage form for Kshatriyas.
entities.justification: The Rakshasa marriage is named, defined, and varna-assigned across Mn_3.21, 3.24, and 3.33.

mentions.quote: the eighth and lowest, the Paiśāca
mentions.role: listed as the lowest of the eight marriage forms

mentions.quote: the Paiśāca and the Āsura must never be performed
mentions.role: declared universally unlawful

mentions.quote: When a man secretly approaches a girl who is sleeping, intoxicated, or mentally disordered, that is the Paiśāca, the eighth and most wicked of marriages.
mentions.role: defined as assault on a vulnerable woman

entities.description: The most wicked of the eight marriage forms, involving a man secretly approaching an unconscious, intoxicated, or mentally disordered girl; named after demons (Pishachas) and declared absolutely forbidden.
entities.justification: The Paishacha marriage is defined in Mn_3.34 and explicitly prohibited in Mn_3.25 as one of two forms that must never be performed.

mentions.quote: The Brāhma, the Daiva, and also the Ārṣa
mentions.role: listed as first of the eight forms

mentions.quote: The gift of a daughter, after decking her and honoring her, to a man learned in the Veda and of good conduct, whom the father himself invites, is declared to be the Brāhma rite.
mentions.role: defined as the highest gift-marriage

mentions.quote: The son of a Brāhmī wife, a doer of good deeds, frees from sin ten ancestors who have gone before, ten descendants who come after, and himself as the twenty-first.
mentions.role: subject of the greatest ancestral-liberation claim

entities.description: The highest of the eight marriage forms, in which a father freely gives his adorned daughter to a Veda-learned man of good conduct, producing offspring credited with liberating twenty-one generations.
entities.justification: The Brahma marriage is defined in Mn_3.27 and its extraordinary ancestral merit enumerated in Mn_3.37, making it a structurally central legal event.

mentions.quote: The Brāhma, the Daiva, and also the Ārṣa
mentions.role: listed second among the eight forms

mentions.quote: The gift of a daughter, after having adorned her, to a priest who is duly officiating at a sacrifice while it is in progress, they call the Daiva rite.
mentions.role: defined as gift to a sacrificial priest

mentions.quote: A son born of a Daiva wife frees seven generations before and seven after
mentions.role: subject of the seven-generation liberation claim

entities.description: The second-ranked marriage form in which a father gives his adorned daughter to a priest officiating at a sacrifice; its offspring is credited with liberating fourteen generations.
entities.justification: The Daiva marriage is defined in Mn_3.28 and its merit assessed in Mn_3.38 as a distinct legal-ritual category.

mentions.quote: The Brāhma, the Daiva, and also the Ārṣa
mentions.role: listed third among the eight forms

mentions.quote: When the father gives away his daughter according to the rule, after receiving from the bridegroom, for the fulfillment of the sacred law, a pair of cattle or two, that is called the Ārṣa rite.
mentions.role: defined as gift-marriage with symbolic cattle exchange

mentions.quote: Some say that the pair of cattle taken in the Ārṣa rite is a bride-price, but that is false
mentions.role: subject of legal controversy over whether it constitutes a sale

entities.description: The third-ranked marriage form involving the father receiving a pair of cattle from the groom as a symbolic token; the text defends it against the charge that this constitutes a bride-sale.
entities.justification: The Arsha marriage is defined in Mn_3.29 and debated in Mn_3.53-54, giving it a legally contested role in chapter 3.

mentions.quote: the Āsura
mentions.role: listed fifth among the eight forms

mentions.quote: the Paiśāca and the Āsura must never be performed
mentions.role: declared universally unlawful

mentions.quote: When the bridegroom receives a maiden after having given, by his own will and as much as he is able, wealth to her kinsmen and to the bride herself, that is called the Āsura rite.
mentions.role: defined as purchase marriage

entities.description: One of the two universally prohibited marriage forms, involving the groom paying wealth to the bride's family and to the bride herself; named after the Asuras (demons) and deemed a sale of the bride.
entities.justification: The Asura marriage is defined in Mn_3.31, prohibited in Mn_3.25, yet paradoxically endorsed for Vaishyas and Shudras in Mn_3.24, creating a textual tension addressed in the chapter.

mentions.quote: the Prājāpatya
mentions.role: name of the fourth marriage form

mentions.quote: The gift of a daughter after honoring the couple and addressing them with the words, 'May you both perform your Dharma together,' is remembered as the Prājāpatya rite.
mentions.role: deity whose name designates this marriage form

mentions.quote: a son of a Kāya (Prājāpatya) wife, six before and six after
mentions.role: source of the twelve-generation liberation claim

entities.description: The lord of creatures (Prajapati) whose name designates the fourth and joint-dharma-oriented marriage form, producing sons credited with liberating twelve generations.
entities.justification: Prajapati is invoked implicitly through the name 'Prājāpatya' as the divine archetype of the marriage-by-equal-dharma-compact in Mn_3.30.

mentions.quote: nor with a Brahmana who has not studied the Veda
mentions.role: qualification criterion for a legitimate guru

mentions.quote: The vow of studying the three Vedas under a guru should be kept for thirty-six years
mentions.role: the canonical body of knowledge defining studentship

mentions.quote: Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda in due order
mentions.role: graduated completion criterion for brahmacharya

mentions.quote: to a man learned in the Veda and of good conduct
mentions.role: qualification criterion for the bridegroom in Brahma marriage

mentions.quote: through failure to study the Veda, and through insults to Brahmanas, families fall from their high state
mentions.role: Vedic study as a pillar sustaining family status

entities.description: The canonical scriptural corpus whose study defines the student stage of life (brahmacharya) and whose mastery qualifies both a guru and a bridegroom in the Brahma marriage.
entities.justification: The Veda functions as the central normative object structuring both studentship rules in chapter 2 and marriage-eligibility rules in chapter 3.

mentions.quote: by attending the sacred fire, he should attain perfection for his soul
mentions.role: ritual substitute for the deceased guru when no surviving relatives remain

entities.description: The perpetual sacrificial fire tended by a student as a ritual focal point that substitutes for a deceased guru's lineage when no kin survive.
entities.justification: The sacred fire is prescribed in Mn_2.248 as the last resort ritual object when all of the guru's family have died, making it a concrete ritual object in the text.

mentions.quote: She who is not a Sapinda of his mother and not of the same Gotra as his father is recommended for the twice-born for marriage
mentions.role: patrilineal descent group whose exogamy rule governs marriage eligibility

entities.description: The patrilineal clan lineage (gotra) whose exogamy is one of the two main kinship criteria for selecting a lawful wife; marriage within the same gotra is prohibited.
entities.justification: Gotra is explicitly invoked in Mn_3.5 as a technical kinship criterion for marriage eligibility, functioning as an organizing legal concept.

mentions.quote: She who is not a Sapinda of his mother and not of the same Gotra as his father is recommended for the twice-born for marriage
mentions.role: matrilineal kinship category whose prohibition limits marriage eligibility

entities.description: The kinship category denoting shared piṇḍa (funeral rice-ball) obligations, i.e., close bilateral relatives; marriage to a Sapinda of one's mother is prohibited.
entities.justification: Sapinda is named as a technical legal concept in Mn_3.5 to define the matrilineal boundary of incest prohibition in marriage.

mentions.quote: A pupil who desires the highest state should not dwell permanently with a non-Brahmana guru
mentions.role: the teacher whose qualifications govern permanent residence

mentions.quote: he should diligently serve him until he is released from his body
mentions.role: object of lifelong devoted service

mentions.quote: A Brahmana who serves his guru until the dissolution of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahma.
mentions.role: the person whose lifelong service secures cosmic reward

mentions.quote: A knower of Dharma should not give any gift to his guru beforehand; but when he is about to take the ceremonial bath, having been permitted by his guru, he should procure a gift for him
mentions.role: recipient of the graduation gift

mentions.quote: When the ācārya has died, he should behave towards his virtuous son, or his wife, or his kinsman as towards the guru himself.
mentions.role: figure whose surviving family inherits the student's devotion

entities.description: The teacher-preceptor (guru/acharya) who is the central social figure in the studentship stage; a student owes him permanent devoted service and graduation gifts, and the devotion extends to his surviving family after death.
entities.justification: The guru is the pivotal relational figure in ch02:241-248, with five distinct verses governing the student's duties to and around him.

themes.topic: Guru devotion as the path to liberation

mentions.quote: A pupil who desires the highest state should not dwell permanently with a non-Brahmana guru, nor with a Brahmana who has not studied the Veda.
if he desires to dwell permanently in his guru's family, he should diligently serve him until he is released from his body.
A Brahmana who serves his guru until the dissolution of his body goes straight to the eternal abode of Brahma.
A Brahmana who thus practices his studentship without breaking his vow goes to the highest abode and is not born here again.

themes.justification: Mn_2.242-249 establish that complete, lifelong guru-service is the supreme path to Brahma's abode and liberation from rebirth, linking pedagogical fidelity directly to soteriological outcomes.

themes.topic: Ritual gifts as the proper completion of studentship

mentions.quote: A knower of Dharma should not give any gift to his guru beforehand; but when he is about to take the ceremonial bath, having been permitted by his guru, he should procure a gift for him according to his ability.
A field, gold, a cow, a horse, an umbrella and shoes, a seat, grain, vegetables, and clothes—he should bring these to please his guru.

themes.justification: Mn_2.245-246 prescribe the timing and enumeration of the graduation gift (dakshina), framing it as the proper ritual closure of brahmacharya.

themes.topic: Varna endogamy and the prohibition of hypogamous marriage

mentions.quote: For the first marriage of the twice-born, a wife of the same varna is recommended
In no sacred text whatsoever is a Shudra woman ordained as a wife for a Brahmana or a Kshatriya
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of a low caste, quickly degrade their families and their descendants to the state of Shudras.
A Shudra woman is for a Shudra; she and one of his own varna for a Vaishya; these two and one of his own varna for a Kshatriya; and these three and one of his own varna for a Brahmana.

themes.justification: Chapter 3's marriage legislation is organized around the principle that same-varna marriage is the norm and that marrying down in varna causes ritual degradation, making varna endogamy the dominant structural theme.

themes.topic: The eight forms of marriage ranked by ritual legitimacy

mentions.quote: Now learn in summary these eight forms of marriage for women, for the four varnas, which are beneficial and harmful in this world and the next.
The Brāhma, the Daiva, and also the Ārṣa; the Prājāpatya and the Āsura; the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa; and the eighth and lowest, the Paiśāca.
But of these five, three are lawful and two are unlawful; the Paiśāca and the Āsura must never be performed.
The sages know that the first four are praiseworthy for a Brahmana, the Rākṣasa alone for a Kshatriya, and the Āsura for a Vaishya and a Shudra.

themes.justification: Mn_3.20-35 constitute a systematic taxonomy of eight marriage forms ordered from most to least ritually legitimate, with different forms assigned to each varna.

themes.topic: Ancestral liberation through the merit of offspring from proper marriages

mentions.quote: The son of a Brāhmī wife, a doer of good deeds, frees from sin ten ancestors who have gone before, ten descendants who come after, and himself as the twenty-first.
A son born of a Daiva wife frees seven generations before and seven after; a son of an Ārṣa wife, three before and three after; and a son of a Kāya (Prājāpatya) wife, six before and six after.
From the first four marriages, in their order—the Brāhma and the others—are born sons who are endowed with spiritual luster and are approved by the virtuous.

themes.justification: Mn_3.37-40 enumerate the precise number of generations that a son's virtuous deeds liberate, making ancestral soteriological benefit a key motivation for choosing the highest-ranked marriage forms.

themes.topic: Honoring women as a condition of family and ritual prosperity

mentions.quote: They should be honored and adorned by their fathers, brothers, husbands, and brothers-in-law, who desire great prosperity.
Where women are honored, there the gods themselves rejoice; but where they are not honored, there all sacred rites are fruitless.
Where the female relatives grieve, that family quickly perishes; but where they do not grieve, that family always prospers.
Those houses which female relatives, not being duly honored, curse, perish completely, as if destroyed by black magic.
In that family where the husband is content with his wife, and the wife is likewise with her husband, there good fortune is assuredly constant.

themes.justification: Mn_3.55-62 constitute a distinct sub-unit on the cosmic-ritual importance of female welfare in the household, linking women's happiness directly to divine approval and family survival.

themes.topic: Sacred knowledge (Veda) as the foundation of family and social status

mentions.quote: Through improper marriages, through neglect of sacred rites, through failure to study the Veda, and through insults to Brahmanas, families fall from their high state.
And by sacrificing for those unworthy to have sacrifices performed for them, and by denial of the efficacy of sacred rites, families that are deficient in sacred knowledge quickly perish.
But families that are rich in sacred knowledge, even if they have little wealth, are counted among the great families and attain great fame.

themes.justification: Mn_3.63-66 close the chapter by identifying Vedic knowledge as the supreme determinant of true family status, explicitly ranking it above material wealth.

themes.topic: The bride-price debate: gift versus sale in the Arsha marriage

mentions.quote: Some say that the pair of cattle taken in the Ārṣa rite is a bride-price, but that is false; whether small or great, it is still a sale.
When kinsmen do not take the price for themselves, that is not a sale; it is merely a token of respect for the maiden and an act of pure kindness.
The learned father of a maiden should not accept even the smallest bride-price; for a man who accepts a price out of greed becomes a seller of his offspring.

themes.justification: Mn_3.51-54 record an implicit debate over whether symbolic cattle exchange in the Arsha marriage constitutes a bride-sale, showing the text's awareness of competing legal interpretations.

themes.topic: Graduated transgenerational moral inheritance from birth quality

mentions.quote: But from the remaining, inferior marriages are born sons who are cruel, speakers of untruth, who hate the Veda and the Dharma.
From unblamed marriages of women, an unblamed progeny is born; from blameworthy ones, a blameworthy progeny is born to men
A male child is produced when the male seed is greater, a female child when the female seed is greater

themes.justification: Mn_3.41-42 and 3.49 reflect an implicit theory of moral-biological inheritance in which the ritual quality of one's conception and birth determines one's moral character, tying reproductive biology to dharmic outcomes.

citations.quote: By marrying a Shudra woman, a Brahmana falls, according to Atri and the son of Utathya
citations.justification: The text explicitly attributes a specific legal ruling on varna-transgressive marriage to the sage Atri, invoking his authority to support the prohibition.

citations.quote: according to Atri and the son of Utathya
citations.justification: The son of Utathya (likely Dīrghatamas) is named alongside Atri as a co-authority for the same ruling on Brahmana degradation through inter-varna marriage.

citations.quote: by begetting a son on her, according to Shaunaka
citations.justification: Shaunaka is cited as a distinct legal authority whose ruling specifies a later threshold for degradation than Atri, indicating awareness of differing scholarly positions.

citations.quote: and by having a son from her, according to Bhrigu
citations.justification: Bhrigu is cited as a fourth authority whose ruling represents the most lenient threshold for full degradation, completing a four-way contrast of expert opinions in a single verse.
